title: why the world looks solid
hookLine: a rope on a dark path, and the snake that was never there
last: DO NO HARM — START WITH YOUR MOUTH.

cards: Dusk, on a path, and something is coiled across it. Your heart jumps before your mind has a word for it. Snake.
You freeze. Your pulse is real. The fear is real.
Then someone brings a lamp, and it's a rope. Just a rope, lying where it always was. Nothing about the rope changed.
The snake was never there. And yet for a few seconds it ran your whole body. Teachers in this tradition tell that small story because it holds a very big word.

teach.h: NOT FAKE. NOT THE WHOLE STORY.
teach.b: Maya. It often gets translated as illusion, and that one word causes a lot of confusion. It sounds like the tradition is saying the world is fake.

Your kitchen, your friends, your job, none of it real. That isn't what it says. The Svetasvatara Upanishad puts it this way: know that nature is maya, and that the great Lord is the one who works the maya.

teach.h: THE POWER THAT MAKES IT APPEAR.
teach.b: It's the power that makes the world appear the way it does, so convincingly that we stop looking past it. Schools of the tradition read this differently, and they've argued about it with great care.

teach.h: SNAKE ON A ROPE, OR GOD'S POWER?
teach.b: Advaita Vedanta, the school of Shankara, says the world we see is an appearance laid over Brahman, the way the snake is laid over the rope. The rope is what's really there.

Other schools, like those of Ramanuja and Madhva, hold that the world is fully real, made by God, and that maya names God's wondrous power. Both readings agree on one thing. The surface is not the whole story.
And that's where the word walks into an ordinary day.

teach.h: A POST. A COMMENT. A BAD MORNING.
teach.b: A post makes someone's life look perfect. A comment feels like an attack on all of you. A bad morning looks like a bad life.
Each one is a snake on the path, until the lamp comes. Neither reading asks anyone to stop living in the world. Only to stop gripping it as if the surface were everything.

how: Hindu teachers explain maya through stories like the rope and the snake, and the schools of Vedanta read it in different ways, some as the appearance of the world over Brahman, others as God's real and wondrous power.

games.q: every time the wifi dies dad sighs 'it's all maya, beta' 🙄 Sam asked if that means Hindus think the world is fake. do we??
o: no. maya is the power that makes the world appear. it's real, it's just not the whole story, like the rope under the snake.
yes, nothing is real, so nothing matters.
maya just means bad luck with technology.
games.why: In the old teaching, a lamp shows that the snake on the path was a rope all along. Maya doesn't make the world fake; it means the surface isn't the whole story, and something deeper, Brahman or God, is underneath.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: the great Lord works the maya

s: maya means the world is fake and doesn't matter
maya isn't nothing. the Svetasvatara Upanishad calls it the power that makes the world appear.
in the rope story, the fear was never really felt
the pulse and the fear were real. what caused them was never there.
in the story, the rope never changed
only the seeing changed. the snake was never there.

games.q: it's dusk, and something is coiled across your path. your heart is pounding. what does the old story say to do?
o: run, and never take this path again.
bring a lamp and look again.
decide it doesn't matter what it is.
games.why: the lamp shows a rope. nothing about the rope changed; only the seeing did. that's the gap the word maya names.

practice: Today's practice: bring the lamp. Breathe once, slowly. Recall one thing this week that made your heart jump.
A message, a look, a number, a picture of someone else's life. Feel the jump again, just a little. Don't push it away.
Now look at it again, slowly, as if someone had brought a lamp. What is actually there? Let the tightness loosen as much as it wants to.

wordCard.voice: Maya. The power that makes the world appear, so well that we stop looking past the surface. The snake that turns out to be rope. Eighteenth word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the power that makes things appear; often translated as illusion.

carryVoice: Your line: hold it lightly. Today, when something makes you jump, take one breath and ask: snake, or rope? Day eighteen.
